seo.title: Karmic tail 18 21 3 compatibility: The Moon, The World, The Empress
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 21 3 compatibility: the rarest couple tail, read through the Song of Songs — a night language, a whole world for two and a vineyard of their own.

title: Karmic tail 18-21-3 in compatibility: from the night dew to a vineyard of one's own
short: 18-21-3 is the rarest of the 97 couple karmic tails: it turns up in roughly one couple in 8,757. The riddle is that it holds no card from outside: The Moon, The World and The Empress already sit in the two partners' personal tails, only in other places. The plot of the tail runs like this: the union begins at night, with a language without words and a secret for two (The Moon), grows into a whole world where nobody else is needed (The World), and the couple's main task is to grow a garden of their own on real ground, in daylight (The Empress).

sections.h2: Why 18-21-3 is the rarest couple tail
paragraphs: A couple's tail is built from two personal tails, and most triples can be built in many ways. 18-21-3 has only one: the personal tails 9-18-9 and 9-3-21, in a hundred per cent of such couples. The second is common, at 2.7% of birth dates: 1,250 dates from 1900 to October 2026. The first is the second rarest of the 26 personal tails: 98 dates in 127 years, 0.21%. Hence one couple in 8,757, 97th place out of 97.

The rarity shows on the calendar itself. The 9-18-9 tail belongs only to people born between January and June, and almost half of those dates, 45 of 98, fall in January. Among people born in the twentieth century it comes down to seven calendar days: 1, 2, 3 and 30 January, 1 and 2 February, 1 March, and not in every year. So in an 18-21-3 couple one partner's birthday always falls in the first half of the year, and if that partner was born before 2000, no later than 1 March.

The second clue is more curious. The couple gets none of the three cards of its tail from outside. The Moon stands twice in the chart of the partner with the 9-18-9 tail: at the centre of the personal matrix and in the middle of the personal tail. The Empress is the middle of the 9-3-21 tail, and The World is its karmic task. Only The Hermit disappears, the card both partners start their personal tails with: two Hermits add up to The Moon, 9 + 9 = 18.

And the third: for one of the two, The Empress and The World come in the personal tail in the order "first The Empress, then The World". In the couple's tail the order is reversed, first a whole world, then the garden. This is not a division of roles: nobody in the couple is "in charge" of a card or to blame for its minus. But something here is familiar to each of them, and it stands in an unfamiliar place.

sections.h2: The Song of Songs: a book that begins and ends with a vineyard
paragraphs: The Song of Songs is eight chapters of a conversation between two people: she and he, a chorus of the daughters of Jerusalem, angry brothers, the night watch. Around the turn of the first and second centuries there was a dispute over whether such a book belonged in Scripture, and Rabbi Akiva answered in a way that settled it: "the whole world is not worth the day on which the Song of Songs was given to Israel, for all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the Holy of Holies" (Mishnah, Yadayim 3:5; our translation). A whole world set against one day of a book about two people: keep these words in mind, because The World stands in the middle of this tail.

The book is closed into a ring. In the first chapter the young woman says: "my mother's children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept" (1:6). In the last: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me" (8:12). In Hebrew both places have the same two words, karmi sheli, "my vineyard, my very own", and they appear nowhere else in the book. Everything in between is the road from someone else's vineyard to one's own.

The most famous interpreter of the Song never reached the end of that road. Bernard of Clairvaux preached 86 sermons on the Song of Songs from 1135 until his death in 1153 and stopped at the start of the third chapter, at the verse "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth". Eighteen years went on the first two chapters, up to the threshold of the night; other abbots finished the commentary for him. For a couple with The Moon at the entry this is an exact parable: the night can take all the time there is if it is only interpreted and not lived.

In 1825 Pushkin made two poems out of the Song, and they were first printed side by side under the shared title "Podrazhaniya" ("Imitations"). The first is a night poem: "V krovi gorit ogon zhelanya…" ("The fire of desire burns in my blood…") ends with the lines "Till the cheerful day breathes / And the night shadow stirs" (literal translation), which is verse 2:17, "Until the day break, and the shadows flee away". The second is a garden poem: "Vertograd moyey sestry, / Vertograd uyedinyonny" ("My sister's garden, / A secluded garden"). Night and garden are the two halves of this tail.

The voices of the Song are a woman's and a man's, but in a couple they are not tied to sex: either partner may fail to open the door at night or search until morning. From here on, card by card. The Moon is the Song's two nights. The World is the garden with all its scents and the road from Lebanon. The Empress is the vineyard that turns from someone else's into one's own.

sections.h2: The Moon at the entry: dew in the hair and a door opened too late
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its common language. In the compatibility reading the same point appears once more, in the sphere "Relationship and common language", labelled "Common language", and for an 18-21-3 couple The Moon stands there as well. There is nothing gloomy about that. Such a couple's language is a night language: talks until three in the morning, a word only the two of them understand, the knack of hearing what was not said. The partner is first of all a friend, as in the Song: "This is my beloved, and this is my friend" (5:16).

There is also an agreement nobody ever said aloud: not to hurry and not to show. In the Song it sounds as a refrain, three times: "that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (2:7, 3:5, 8:4; the Hebrew says simply "love"). The couple tells no one about itself for a long time and guards the union like a sleep it is afraid to disturb. Wen sees in The Moon "a strong theme of conservation in the card, rather than exploration or expansion", a need for protection and beneath it "a profound vulnerability that the Seeker is trying to conceal from others".

The Song describes The Moon's resistance better than any textbook. "I sleep, but my heart waketh," she says, and that is the lunar state exactly: a half-sleep in which everything is felt and nothing is done. He knocks: "Open to me… for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night." And her answer is not "no" but "later": "I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on?" When at last she gets up and opens, "my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone" (5:2–6).

In a couple's life this looks ordinary. One partner comes home late with a real step: a flat found, a wish to meet the parents, readiness to say aloud that this is serious. The other feels warm and quiet in what already exists and answers: "Not tonight." In the morning the first is polite and distant, and the second spends the whole day looking for what went wrong: rereading messages, catching the tone, inventing versions. The Song knows this sequel too: "I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer."

The night search hurts. "The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me" (5:7). A couple has no shortage of watchmen: other people's opinions, friends' advice, their own guesses that turn into "facts" by morning. Even Solomon's wedding litter in the Song is surrounded by sixty warriors, and "every man hath his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night" (3:8). A fear that guards the union, with its checks, jealousy of things imagined and hurt over things that never happened, is the main minus of the lunar entry.

The Moon has another trap: a light that shows no spots. "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (4:7). Yet in the first chapter she knows otherwise about herself: "I am black, but comely… Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me" (1:5–6). The Moon gives the couple an image without a flaw, and the first flaw seen by day, a lateness, a sharp word, tiredness, feels like a deception. The partner deceived no one: the image was reflected light.

sections.h2: The World in the middle: a garden that needs the wind
paragraphs: The middle of the task is our reading: how the couple walks from the wish at the entry to the main task. For 18-21-3 that road is The World, the card of wholeness. The union stops being a night-time secret and becomes a whole world, with its own roads, its own philosophy, its own places to come back to. Waite's divinatory list for The World reads "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place", and the Song is full of this movement: "Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon… from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards" (4:8). The middle of such a tail may run on the road: a move to another city or country, travel, life between two homes.

The strong side of this middle is wholeness. The two accept each other entirely, talk about everything, argue and find a compromise, see the world the same way. They find each other so interesting that the rest of the world begins to seem optional. And that is where the minus begins.

The garden of the Song is a world inside one fence: pomegranates, spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, myrrh and aloes "with all the chief spices" (4:13–14). But the description opens with "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed" (4:12). That is how the couple's world looks in the minus: everything is there, and everything is locked. Friends stop calling because nobody invites them. One partner reshapes the other to fit "our" worldview. The days are all alike, and in that sameness the unsaid piles up. Sometimes the circle breaks and closes again, and the Song knows this on-again, off-again rhythm: "I held him, and would not let him go" (3:4), then "my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone" (5:6).

If "our world" rests on bans, on not seeing friends and family, reporting every step, being afraid of the other's reaction, this is no longer a matter of cards. It calls for help from living people: a psychologist, a crisis line, and in case of threat a local emergency number.

The Song gives the way out in the very next verse: "Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out" (4:16). A garden does not stop being a garden when the wind blows into it; it begins to smell. Straight after this comes the first invitation to guests: "eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved" (5:1). Pushkin's "Vertograd" puts it even more briefly: "Let but the north wind blow, / And the scents will drip" (literal translation). This couple's world becomes whole not when it holds everything, but when it is open to the north and to the south.

The number of the middle says the same. 21 = 18 + 3: the couple's World is the exact sum of the other two cards of the tail, The Moon and The Empress, with no folding. And in the personal tails it is built from two middles: one partner's Empress and the other's Moon, 3 + 18. The middle of this union is what happens when night and garden meet.

sections.h2: The Empress as the main task: from someone else's vineyard to one's own
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read above all through the minus, through what does not work and what has to be learned. The Empress is the card of fruitfulness, household and home. The task of 18-21-3 is not to love more: this couple has love to spare from the very start. The task is to make it into ground of their own.

The Song itself begins with The Empress's minus. The young woman has been scorched by the sun because her brothers set her to guard other people's vineyards, and her own was left untended. In a couple this looks like weekends at the parents' dacha (the family's country plot), loans from the parents for every big purchase, a mother with keys to the flat, and a flat rented "for now", six years running. Both work hard, and all of it in other people's gardens.

Mothers are everywhere in the Song. The beloved is brought "into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me" (3:4). Solomon's wedding crown is put on him by his mother (3:11). Even the dream in the last chapter is "I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house" (8:2). And the only home of their own in the book stands under the open sky: "also our bed is green. The beams of our house are cedar, and our rafters of fir" (1:16–17). Wen, writing of The Empress reversed, names outright relations "with a mother or mother figure that is strained, experiencing conflict, or in need of the Seeker's attention". To come out from under the family's wing without cutting the tie is the first part of the main task.

The word "our" is first used of the vineyards when they need protecting: "Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes" (2:15; in the Hebrew, "our vineyards are in blossom"). Little foxes are small night animals, and the harm they do is small: an unwashed cup, a forgotten call, a phone at dinner, "I did ask". But blossom is the most fragile time of a garden. The first year of a shared home is spoiled not by great disasters but by little foxes nobody catches, because "it's only a trifle".

The best-known verse of the Song is read at weddings by halves. "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death", and then: "jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire" (8:6). In The Empress, jealousy is part of the lesson: where something of one's own grows, the fear of losing it appears. It matters more for the couple not to pretend the second half of the verse is not there, and to talk about it aloud before it turns to fire.

Money is here too. "If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned" (8:7): love cannot be bought, which is worth remembering in a couple where one earns more. But the next verses are almost bookkeeping. Solomon's vineyard at Baalhamon is let out to keepers, and "every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver"; "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred" (8:11–12). The woman who was set to keep at the start knows the price of keepers at the end: in Hebrew, 1:6 and 8:11–12 use one and the same root, "to keep". What saves a couple from feast or famine is not love but knowing its own numbers. This is exactly what The Empress teaches the couple: love is not counted, but the vineyard is.

The last argument is with the brothers. "We have a little sister… If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she be a door, we will inclose her with boards of cedar" (8:8–9). The family decides who she is and what to do with her. The answer is one sentence: "I am a wall… then was I in his eyes as one that found favour" (8:10). In Hebrew "wall" is the same word as in the night scene, where "the keepers of the walls" tore away her veil. The walls she feared at night are now herself. This is what leaving childishness behind looks like in The Empress: the couple stops being "still little" in the family's eyes and becomes its own protection.

"As one that found favour" reads in the original "as one who finds shalom", that is, peace, and in Russian the name of the middle card, Mir, means both "world" and "peace". The next verse begins with Solomon's name, Shlomo, which has the same ring. The World from the middle of the tail comes back at its end, no longer as a road but as rest: the vineyard is before her, and in the beloved's eyes there is peace.

sections.h2: The Moon, The World and The Empress in Waite and Wen
paragraphs: Waite's Moon is usually read through fear and deception, and his divinatory list does contain "darkness, terror, deception", with "silence" among the reversed meanings. But in describing the older cards he notes a detail that changes the whole entry of this tail: in nearly all versions the moon is "shedding the moisture of fertilizing dew in great drops". The night dew is not only mist; it is the watering of a future garden. The beloved in the Song stands at the door with that dew in his hair. On Waite's card the moon is waxing, "increasing on what is called the side of mercy". Wen calls The Moon "poetry and mystery", and nothing fits the Song more closely.

Waite describes the garland around the figure of The World "as if it were a chain of flowers intended to symbolize all sensible things", and the card itself as "joy attained in the body", "the soul's intoxication in the earthly paradise, but still guarded by the Divine Watchers". That is almost a summary of the Song: a garden with all its scents, "eat, O friends; drink", and there are watchers in it too, only nocturnal and cruel. The figure on the card is dancing, and the Shulammite is asked to turn round and is watched "as upon the dance of Mahanaim" (6:13 in English Bibles, 7:1 in Hebrew; Revised Version). The World's list contains "flight", and the last word of the book is "Make haste, my beloved" (8:14), in Hebrew literally "flee". Reversed, Waite's World is "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence": the locked garden itself. Wen calls The World "the card of synthesis".

Waite's Empress is "the inferior Garden of Eden, the Earthly Paradise"; "A field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water." The Song says of the bride "thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies" (7:2), and of her garden "a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon" (4:15). Wen adds the pomegranates on her robe, which "represent fertility, love, marriage, and passion"; the Song names pomegranates six times. "Earthly paradise" appears twice in Waite: in The World the soul is intoxicated in the earthly paradise, and The Empress is that paradise. The middle of the tail is walking in the garden; the main task is to become the garden.

The main clue hides in two quotations. Waite describes The Empress in the words of the Apocalypse: "Her diadem is of twelve stars", she is "the woman clothed with the sun". That is Revelation 12:1, and between the sun and the stars the verse has a third detail that Waite did not repeat: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars". The card of this couple's main task stands on the card of its entry. The Moon need not be abolished; it is something to stand on. The bride in the Song, by the way, is compared with both lights at once: "fair as the moon, clear as the sun" (6:10). And one more coincidence of words: Waite calls The Empress "the veil of the Sanctum Sanctorum", and Rabbi Akiva called the Song of Songs itself the Holy of Holies.

sections.h2: The couple's centre and values: The Lovers, and The Moon again
paragraphs: The atmosphere inside the couple, its centre, is the same in every 18-21-3 couple: The Lovers. This is the card of choice, and the Song has a formula of choice that sounds three times, differently each time: "My beloved is mine, and I am his" (2:16), then "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" (6:3), and at last "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me" (7:10). First "he is mine", then "I am his", and at the end "he is mine" disappears altogether: what remains is "I belong" and his desire turned towards me. The atmosphere of this couple is a choice made again and again, not a possession received once.

There is a tension between the centre and the entry. The Moon loves a secret, while The Lovers in the plus mean sincerity, trust and no secrets. Inside the couple the night language has to become intimacy, not a way of hiding from each other. In the minus The Lovers bring "now peace, now war", the same swing as the locked garden.

The centre of this tail is no accident. Add up the three cards of the tail, 18 + 21 + 3 = 42 → 6, and the result is The Lovers again. And the centre is built from the two personal centres: for the partner with the 9-3-21 tail it is always 6, for the partner with 9-18-9 always 18, and 6 + 18 = 24 → 6. The Moon from one partner's centre stands at the couple's entry, The Lovers from the other's centre at the couple's centre.

One more check, by the personal formula. In a person's tail the entry equals the karmic task plus the centre. For the couple, 3 + 6 = 9: by that formula the entry would be The Hermit, the very card each of the two starts a personal tail with. Instead it is The Moon, 9 + 9. The couple begins not with each one's solitude but with their shared night.

"The couple's values" are what the union exists for. In 87.9% of 18-21-3 couples The Moon stands there again, and then it appears twice in the matrix: at the entry and in the values. For such a couple the night is not only a door but a meaning: depth, mystery, a language without words, a world that needs no explaining to outsiders. The task is not to give this up but to stand on it, as The Empress stands on the moon. In the remaining 12.1% the values hold The Hermit: a union for the sake of quiet for two, a lantern for each and slow steps. The personal values of both partners are almost always The Hermit: always for the partner with 9-18-9, and in 88% of cases for the other. In 76.7% of couples two people with The Hermit in their personal values get The Moon in the couple's values.
Two dates for which the site's engine gives this tail. First the personal matrices, then the couple.

head: Point
Couple
rows: D · karmic task, for the couple the main task

paragraphs: This couple has The Hermit in its values: an example from that 12.1%. Both partners were born in the first days of January, four years less a day apart: the calendar clue itself. In other spheres of the reading they have The Hierophant in "Image of the couple" (2 + 3 = 5) and The High Priestess in "What to create together" (1 + 1 = 2), and The Moon returns in "Common language".

sections.h2: How the couple leaves the tail
paragraphs: The strong version of 18-21-3 gives up neither the night nor the whole world. It brings them down to earth: the night language becomes intimacy, their own world becomes an open garden, and the garden becomes their own, with a boundary, a budget and decisions made by two.

ul: **Open while the dew is in the hair.** Answer the partner's real step the same evening, even with a word: "yes", "I'm scared", "let's talk it over on Saturday". "Later" is the politest way to close a door.
**Check the night versions by day.** Separate what is known from what is imagined, and ask rather than search the streets. Reflected light is not evidence.
**Invite the wind into the garden.** Friends, family, new people, shared projects with others, regularly and by choice, so that the world for two gives off its scent instead of locking itself in.
**Catch the little foxes while they are small.** Name small irritations aloud the same day instead of storing them up.
**Count the thousand and the two hundred.** Know the couple's money: what is shared, what belongs to each, how much goes to the "keepers": rent, debts, help to the family.
**Say "I am a wall".** Make decisions about the home, money and plans together and tell the family what has been decided, instead of putting it to a family council.
**Read verse 8:6 to the end.** Jealousy is not love's disgrace but its second half; it is talked about before it turns to fire.

paragraphs: The Song of Songs ends not with a wedding but with the word "Make haste", that is, "flee": the book stays open, and the couple's nights do not end for good. What changes is where they stand. At the start the young woman guards other people's vineyards and looks for her beloved in the streets. At the end she says what the 18-21-3 couple walks its road for: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me."

ul: **M · Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** This is the wish the couple enters the task with: to understand each other without words, to keep the union from other people's eyes, to live on night-time talk. The same Moon also resists: things left unsaid, hurts made up in the head, a partner seen without a single spot.

**N · Middle of the task — 21, The World.** This is how the couple walks the road: the union becomes a whole world, with its own roads, moves, circle and philosophy. In the minus, that world locks itself from the inside.

**D · Main task — 3, The Empress.** To turn a night-time union into a home of their own: to decide together without looking over their shoulder at the family, to know their own money, to grow something shared and to stop guarding other people's vineyards.

intro: The right-hand column shows where each number comes from. A couple's point is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, and in couples with this tail the personal tails are always the same: 9-18-9 for one partner and 9-3-21 for the other. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers: 18-21-3 is the only order.

The key to the plot lies in the best-known book about two people, the Song of Songs. It opens with a complaint, "mine own vineyard have I not kept", and closes with the words "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". Between them come two nights of searching, a garden with all the scents of the world and an argument with the brothers over whether the bride has grown up. That is the 18-21-3 tail, written down long before the destiny matrix.

faq.q: Is 18-21-3 a programme in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: Yes, if it is a couple's matrix: Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail exactly that, the couple's karmic programme. It is read in the order "entry to the task, middle, main task": The Moon, The World, The Empress. A single person's matrix never has an 18-21-3 karmic tail.

faq.q: Can 18-21-3 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: Not as a tail. In a person's chart the entry equals the karmic task plus the centre, and with a task of 3 an entry of 18 would need a centre of 15, which no person has. But the same three numbers do appear as lines: an 18-21-3 money line in 0.55% of birth dates, an 18-21-3 relationship line in 0.29%. These are different points, and they are read differently from a couple's tail.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. 18-21-3 is the only order of these three numbers among the 97 couple tails; it has no permutations.

faq.q: How can a couple tell it has this tail without a calculator?
faq.a: For each partner, add up the arcana of the day, month and year of birth, first folding a day above 22 and a year's digit sum above 22. If one partner gets exactly 9 and the other exactly 21, the couple's tail is 18-21-3. Together 9 and 21 make 30 → 3, The Empress of the main task.

faq.q: Does the 18-21-3 tail mean poor compatibility?
faq.a: No. The tail shows the couple's task, not a verdict, and the method gives no compatibility percentages. Rarity does not mean difficulty either: this couple has a strong entry, and all three cards of its tail are already familiar to the two of them.

report: Waite describes The Empress in the words of the Apocalypse: "the woman clothed with the sun", "Her diadem is of twelve stars". Between those words the same verse holds a third detail that he did not repeat: "the moon under her feet". The 18-21-3 tail is built exactly the same way. The couple enters the task through The Moon, walks it through The World, and the main task, The Empress, stands on that Moon. The night is not abolished here. **It is something to stand on.**

The plot of this tail is written in the Song of Songs, the best-known book about two people. It begins with the complaint "mine own vineyard have I not kept" and ends with the words "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". In Hebrew both places have the same two words, karmi sheli, and they appear nowhere else in the book. **The couple's whole road runs from someone else's vineyard to its own.**

Friends stop calling because nobody invites them, one partner reshapes the other to fit "our" worldview, the days are all alike. If "our world" rests on bans, on not seeing close people, reporting every step, being afraid of the other's reaction, this is no longer a matter of cards but a reason to turn to a psychologist or a crisis line, and in case of threat to a local emergency number.

The way out stands in the very next verse: "Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out." Straight after it comes the first invitation to guests: "eat, O friends; drink". **A garden does not stop being a garden when the wind blows into it: it begins to smell.**

report.h3: From someone else's vineyard to its own

report: The main task is The Empress, and it is read through the minus. At the start of the Song the young woman has been scorched by the sun because her brothers set her to guard other people's vineyards. In a couple this means weekends at the parents' dacha, loans from the parents, a mother with keys to the flat and a home rented "for now", six years running. Mothers are everywhere in the Song: even Solomon's wedding crown is put on him by his mother.

The vineyards are first called "ours" when they need protecting: "Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes." The first year of a shared home is spoiled not by great disasters but by little foxes: an unwashed cup, a forgotten call, "I did ask".

The best-known verse of the book is read at weddings by halves: "love is strong as death", and then "jealousy is cruel as the grave". And at the end of the Song comes something close to bookkeeping: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred." **Love is not counted, but the vineyard is.**

The last argument is with the brothers: "We have a little sister… If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver." The answer is one sentence: "I am a wall… then was I in his eyes as one that found favour." In Hebrew "wall" is the same word as in the night scene, where "the keepers of the walls" tore away her veil. The walls that were feared at night become the couple itself. And "favour" in the original is shalom, peace, which in Russian shares its name, Mir, with the card of the middle: The World comes back at the end, no longer as a road but as rest.
The strong version of the tail gives up neither the night nor the whole world, but brings them down to earth:

ul: answer the partner's real step the same evening, even with a word;
check the night versions by day, separating what is known from what is imagined;
invite friends and family into the couple's world by choice;
catch the little foxes while they are small;
know the couple's money and decide about the home together, telling the family what has already been decided.

report: At the start of the Song the young woman guards other people's vineyards and looks for her beloved in the night streets. At the end she says what the 18-21-3 couple walks its road for: **"My vineyard, which is mine, is before me."**
